implementation_notes: Scala 2.13 ships the scheme in the standard library: Iterator.unfold takes a function from state to Option[(element, nextState)] and returns a lazy Iterator ending when the function returns None. It is the right default for one-pass pipelines because nothing is retained beyond the current element, at the price of single use; effectful or fused generation is covered by fs2 Stream.unfold and cats.
code_sketch:
val countdown: Iterator[Int] =
  Iterator.unfold(8)(s => if (s > 1) Some((s, s / 2)) else None)
countdown.take(3).toList   // List(8, 4, 2)
pitfalls: Iterator is single-use: once consumed it is empty, so a second toList returns Nil instead of replaying the unfold.
An Option that is always Some yields an infinite structure; takeWhile outside is not a substitute for a stop condition inside the step function.

variants.name: LazyList.unfold (memoising coinductive list)
variants.implementation_notes: The same standard-library signature producing a LazyList: elements are computed on first demand and then retained, so the structure can be traversed repeatedly and can be infinite without recomputation. Choose it when the unfold is a corecursive value to be revisited and retention is acceptable; choose Iterator when it is a one-pass pipeline.
variants.code_sketch:
val powers: LazyList[Int] =
  LazyList.unfold(1)(s => if (s < 100) Some((s, s * 2)) else None)
powers.take(3).toList   // List(1, 2, 4) - values are memoised
pitfalls: Retaining the head of a LazyList keeps every computed element and its captured state alive, which is a classic space leak for large or endless unfolds.
Effects inside the step function are memoised with the elements, so a side-effecting generator runs at most once per element.
